WRHBA is here this morning to voice our strong support
for Councillor Craig motion,
calling for a fulsome independent investigation
to the origins of the region's current water supply and capacity constraint, along with
the recommendations to strengthen oversight moving forward.
Water is among the region's most essential public responsibilities.
Residents, businesses, and municipal partners all rely on transparent, forward-looking planning
to ensure that growth is supported by infrastructure that is resilient, safe, and responsibly managed.
Like with many situations in life, we can't know where we're going unless we know where we've been.
It is clear that the current constraint has roots, at least partially, in the understanding of the integrated water supply system and the methodology implemented for monitoring that system.
The emergency of a water capacity constraint of this scale, with virtually no prior indication of an emerging issue, has raised understandable concerns across the community.
Residents and businesses deserve clarity on how this situation developed, whether warning
signs were missed, and what systemic improvements are needed to prevent similar issues in the
future.
An independent, arm's length review is the most effective way to restore public confidence.
Such an investigation can objectively assess the decision-making processes, data assumptions,
structures and resources that contributed to the present constraint. Importantly, it can also
highlight opportunities to modernize oversight, strengthen internal accountability, and improve
communication among regional departments, local municipalities, and the public. This is not about
assigning blame. It is about ensuring that our systems are robust, transparent, and capable of
supporting the region's long-term security. The motion before you today reflects a commitment
to responsible stewardship and good governance. At the same time, the consequences of a
development freeze are not abstract. WRHBA, together with Build Urban, the Grand Valley
Construction Association, and other large community organizations is in process of
retaining an independent economic consultant to quantify the social and economic costs associated
with a prolonged inability to bring new housing and employment-related development forward.
This work is being conducted entirely at industry cost but for the sole purpose of ensuring that
Council fully understands the broad community-wide impacts of inaction and why a timely
transparent resolution to the water constraint is essential. Embracing an external review will help
ensure that future growth, whether it be housing, economic development, or public services,
precedes confidence in the region's infrastructure planning. So for those reasons, we urge Council to
support Agenda Item 6.1 and move forward with a comprehensive independent investigation and
and subsequent recommendations for a stronger oversight of the water.
